answer.rationale: Constraints dominate: 14 days to expiry, 94% utilization with no buffer, and only one decision this cycle. A primary-vendor switch (memory_c2) is the only path with headline unit-cost savings large enough to plausibly reach 18%, but that same record explicitly warns the low-cost vendor missed the delivery SLA in three of four quarters and must not be sole source on a critical line — which is exactly what a switch would create here. Adding a second source (memory_c3) is the right structural move but takes qualification time the 14-day window does not allow, and it does not by itself cut spend. Deferring (memory_c5) worked on a non-critical renewal on month-to-month terms; this contract does not auto-renew, so deferral means running the committed line without a contract. That leaves negotiate_terms: memory_c4 shows benchmarking against market rates moved the incumbent on both price and payment terms, and memory_c2 supplies the credible benchmark to negotiate against without taking on its delivery risk. Memory_c1 supports continuity value (no migration work). I want the archive for memory_c2 to check whether the cost delta is current and whether the SLA misses were volume-related or systemic, and for memory_c4 to see the actual magnitude recovered — if it was mid-single-digit, negotiation alone will not clear an 18% mandate and I should report the gap rather than manufacture it. I am deliberately not pursuing the multi-year volume commitment in memory_c6 this cycle: locking a long term before a second source exists would foreclose the dual-sourcing option that memory_c3 shows is what actually protected allocation during a shortage.
